title: The Dot-Com Bubble by the Numbers (and the 2026 Echo)
note: EP042 — explainer (By the Numbers, row 32). The 1995–2000 dot-com bubble: internet mania, 'eyeballs' over profits, IPO frenzy, the Nasdaq's March 2000 peak and ~78% crash, survivors like Amazon — and the 2026 AI echo. Real portraits (Greenspan, Bezos). 5 new motifs (dotcompeak, eyeballs, burnrate, profitlessvaluation, bubbleecho) + doodles (dialup, sockpuppet). Target 12–15 min.

scenes.narration: In 1999, a company whose main asset was a sock puppet went public and was briefly worth over three hundred million dollars. It had barely any revenue, and enormous losses. Nine months later, it was gone.
That company, Pets.com, became the mascot of an era of collective financial insanity — when the whole world briefly agreed that profits didn't matter, as long as you had a dot-com in your name.

scenes.memeBottom: '…but we'll make it up on volume!'
scenes.narration: It produced one of the biggest stock bubbles in history — and, twenty-five years later, a lot of people are nervously asking if we're watching it happen all over again.
The event was the dot-com bubble — a stock market bubble that developed in the late 1990s and peaked on March tenth, 2000.
It arguably began in 1995, when a young browser company called Netscape went public. It had tiny revenues and no profits — and its stock nearly tripled on day one. Wall Street had found a new drug.
To see the madness, you first have to feel the genuine excitement underneath it.
scenes.heading: The Mania

scenes.narration: In the late 1990s, the internet arrived in people's homes, and it really was world-changing. Everyone could feel it: this would transform shopping, media, communication — everything.
And that part was absolutely true. The mistake wasn't believing in the internet. The mistake was believing that every single company with a website was therefore going to be worth a fortune.
What took hold was a classic economic bubble — a period when asset prices greatly exceed their intrinsic, fundamentals-based valuation.
Money poured in. Venture capitalists threw cash at anything with a dot-com plan, desperate not to miss the next big thing — a feeding frenzy of fear of missing out.
The fever spread to Main Street. Ordinary people quit their jobs to become day traders, glued to screens, convinced that flipping internet stocks from their bedroom was a reliable path to riches.
The fuel was venture capital — financing provided by firms to startup and early-stage companies deemed to have high growth potential.
The result was a stock chart that looked less like investing and more like a rocket launch.
scenes.heading: The Peak

scenes.narration: These companies mostly listed on the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange. And as the mania built, the Nasdaq didn't just rise — it went vertical, roughly five-folding in a handful of years.
That exchange was the Nasdaq — the first fully electronic stock market, and the natural home for the new internet darlings.
It peaked on March tenth, 2000, at just over five thousand. Everyone assumed it was just getting started. Instead, that was the top — and from there, it fell roughly seventy-eight percent.
scenes.caption: the Nasdaq fell about 78%

scenes.title: Nasdaq index level
scenes.narration: Put the scale in numbers. The Nasdaq peaked above five thousand in March 2000, crashed to around a thousand — and did not reclaim that peak for about fifteen years.
So how did anyone justify these prices? They invented a whole new kind of math.
scenes.heading: The New Math

scenes.narration: Normally you value a company on its profits. But these companies had no profits — only losses. So Wall Street simply stopped looking at profits, and started valuing 'eyeballs' and 'clicks' instead.
The logic was: get as many users as possible now, and the money will magically appear later. So user numbers soared into the sky, while actual profits stayed flat on the floor.
scenes.caption: clicks soared, profits never came

scenes.narration: The casualties became legends. Webvan raised over a billion dollars to deliver groceries, and collapsed. The fashion site Boo-dot-com burned through roughly a hundred and thirty-five million in just eighteen months.
This led to companies worth billions of dollars that had never made a cent — and had no clear plan to ever do so. Price had completely detached from reality.
A startup could be valued at ten billion dollars with a profit of exactly zero. The number in the valuation and the number in the bank account had nothing to do with each other.
scenes.caption: billion-dollar price, zero profit

scenes.narration: The IPO pops became cartoonish. One company, theGlobe-dot-com, saw its stock rocket more than six hundred percent on its first day of trading — for a business almost nobody could explain.
And the companies happily played along, burning through the cash as fast as investors could shovel it in.
scenes.heading: Get Big Fast

scenes.narration: The mantra was 'get big fast.' Grab market share at any cost — give products away, spend wildly on advertising — and worry about making money some other day. The result was a spectacular burn rate.
Startups were torching tens of millions of dollars a year with no profit in sight. As long as new investor money kept flooding in, the fire could keep burning. The moment it stopped, they were dead.
scenes.caption: burning millions, earning nothing

scenes.narration: Nothing captured the madness like the 2000 Super Bowl. More than a dozen dot-coms paid millions each for ads. Within two years, most of those companies simply no longer existed.

props.name: stockscreen
props.label: a graveyard of Super Bowl ads

scenes.narration: Fueling it all was a frenzy of IPOs — initial public offerings, where a company's shares are sold to institutional and retail investors for the first time.
Dot-com IPOs routinely doubled or tripled on their very first day of trading. Ordinary people, terrified of missing the next Microsoft, piled into companies they didn't understand at all.

scenes.memeBottom: still have no way to make money
scenes.narration: The business plan, for an alarming number of these companies, genuinely ended at 'and then we IPO.' The part where they actually earned a profit was simply left blank.
Companies discovered that simply adding 'dot-com' to their name could send their stock soaring — regardless of what they actually did.
A few people did try to warn everyone. They were comprehensively ignored.
scenes.heading: The Warning

scenes.label: ALAN GREENSPAN
scenes.caption: warned in 1996 — ignored for years
scenes.narration: Back in 1996, years before the peak, Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan gave a speech wondering whether markets had been gripped by 'irrational exuberance.'
That very phrase — 'irrational exuberance' — entered history, used by Greenspan to question whether asset prices had detached from reality.
In the end, two things pricked it. The Federal Reserve raised interest rates, making easy money scarce — and a landmark antitrust ruling against Microsoft rattled the whole tech sector's nerves.
But the party was far too much fun to stop. The market shrugged off the warning and kept climbing for more than three more years. In a mania, being early and being wrong feel exactly the same.
Then, in the spring of 2000, reality finally sent its invoice.
scenes.heading: The Pop

scenes.narration: Sentiment simply turned. Interest rates ticked up, a few darlings missed their targets, and investors suddenly remembered to ask a dangerous question: wait, when exactly do these companies make money?
Once that doubt crept in, the new money stopped flowing. And for companies that survived purely on new money, that was instantly fatal. The cash ran out, and they started dropping like flies.
From its peak, the Nasdaq lost about seventy-eight percent of its value over the next two and a half years. Trillions of dollars of paper wealth simply evaporated.
Around five trillion dollars in market value was ultimately wiped out. And remember: the Nasdaq took roughly fifteen years just to climb back to where it had been at the peak.
Pets.com, Webvan, Boo-dot-com — hundreds of once-glamorous startups went bankrupt, often within months. The sock puppet went from Super Bowl star to punchline in under a year.

Pets.com is the perfect epitaph. A famous sock-puppet mascot, a multi-million-dollar Super Bowl ad, an IPO in February 2000 — and the lights switched off for good by that November. Nine months, start to finish.

scenes.memeTop: the pitch deck: the future of retail
scenes.memeBottom: the reality: a bankrupt sock puppet
scenes.narration: The gap between the dazzling story and the grim arithmetic was enormous — and, for a while, almost nobody wanted to measure it.
But here's the twist that makes this story so important: the internet still won.
scenes.heading: The Survivors

scenes.narration: The technology was never the lie. The web really did go on to transform the world. The bubble was about price and timing — not about whether the internet mattered. It mattered enormously.

scenes.label: JEFF BEZOS
scenes.caption: Amazon fell ~90% — and survived
scenes.narration: Amazon's stock crashed by around ninety percent in the bust. Many wrote it off for dead. Instead, Jeff Bezos's company survived, kept building, and became one of the most valuable firms on Earth.
That's the pattern after every tech bubble. The flood of money builds real things — networks, companies, infrastructure — and from the wreckage, a few genuine giants emerge to inherit the future.

And the wasted money wasn't entirely wasted. Telecom firms laid vast amounts of fiber-optic cable that mostly went bankrupt — but that 'dark fiber' later became the cheap backbone of the modern internet.
And some of the biggest winners weren't even there yet. Google was founded in 1998 but didn't go public until 2004 — rising from the ashes, long after the first-movers had burned out.
Which brings us, nervously, to right now.
scenes.heading: The 2026 Echo

scenes.narration: Today we're living through the AI boom — a period of rapid growth in artificial intelligence, accelerating through the 2020s.

And the AI echo has its own eye-watering numbers. Trillions in planned data-center spending, chipmakers worth more than entire economies, and a tangle of circular deals where the same few giants fund each other.

And the parallels are impossible to ignore. A genuine, world-changing technology. Giddy investors. Sky-high valuations for companies with little or no profit. And 'AI' being bolted onto any pitch to attract cash.
History, as they say, doesn't repeat — but it often rhymes. Lay the two charts side by side, and the rhythm of hype, surge, and detachment looks uncomfortably familiar.
scenes.caption: history doesn't repeat — it rhymes

scenes.title: Dot-com, 1995–2015
scenes.narration: The full cycle took twenty years. Netscape in 1995. Greenspan's warning in 1996. The peak in March 2000. The long crash. Google's IPO in 2004. And a full recovery only around 2015.

scenes.memeBottom: know in advance when the music stops
scenes.narration: The cruel part is that nobody rings a bell at the top. In the moment, a bubble and a genuine boom feel exactly, identically the same.

scenes.memeBottom: therefore THIS pet-food website is worth billions
scenes.narration: The dangerous leap is always the same: a true belief about a technology gets stretched into an insane belief about a specific stock's price.
So how do you tell a real revolution from a bubble? The uncomfortable answer: it can be both.
scenes.heading: The Lesson

scenes.narration: This is the key insight people miss. The internet was real and the dot-com stocks were a bubble, at the exact same time. A technology can change the world while the stocks built on it still crash eighty percent.

props.name: scale
props.label: both can be true at once

scenes.narration: This is why even the smartest investors get trapped. They're right about the technology, so they feel justified paying any price — and 'the internet is huge' becomes an excuse for owning a stock at a hundred times a profit it doesn't have.

scenes.memeBottom: a great technology does not make an overpriced stock a good investment
scenes.narration: Being right about the future is not the same as making money. You can be completely correct that a technology will win, and still lose a fortune paying the wrong price for it.

So the napkin test is timeless. Strip away the story and ask: how does this company actually make money, and is the price I'm paying sane relative to that? If the only answer is 'growth,' tread very carefully.

The practical defenses are boring but powerful. Spread your bets instead of betting the farm on one hot name. Keep buying steadily rather than piling in at the peak. And never invest money you can't afford to see halve.
And watch for the tell-tale signs of mania: profitless darlings, a buzzword glued onto every pitch, IPOs that pop for no reason, and the smug certainty that 'this time really is different.'
So let's total up the bubble.
scenes.heading: The Final Math

scenes.narration: A real revolution. Profitless companies valued in the billions. A market that five-folded, then fell seventy-eight percent. Most startups died — but the technology, and a few survivors, changed the world.
The dot-com bubble is the perfect lesson because both halves are true. The believers were right about the internet — and still lost everything by paying insane prices at the top.

So whether today's AI wave is a true golden age, a giant bubble, or — most likely — both at once, the discipline is the same one from 2000: believe in the technology, but never stop asking about the price.
We actually did a whole episode on the AI bubble and the hidden debt propping it up. The echoes with the year 2000 are loud — even if the timing, as always, is impossible to call.
Because gravity always sends its invoice eventually. The only question is whether you'll be holding the sock puppet when it does.
